Divine Providence Governing the Whole Universe

Trithemius argues from Scripture and natural-philosophical reasoning that divine providence governs all things, from birds and grass to the structure of the cosmos, leaving no place for chance against God’s will.

I remember having answered this question as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth, and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence,^1 by whose will and command they were brought forth into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the entire universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion, first from the Scriptures and then by arguments, as briefly as is permitted. In the book of Judith^2 we read: “All your ways are prepared, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the wisest king Solomon^3 speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth so as to make your soul sin, and do not say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered against your words, destroy all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies to providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel,^4 when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and not one of them falls upon the earth before God?”^5 This is a great commendation of divine wisdom: it has care not only for human beings, but even for birds, however tiny. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.”^6 And a little later he adds: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?”^7 Almighty God, because he created all things and brought them forth into being when they did not exist, rules and governs the universe so that it may not collapse and flow away; and he could in no way do this if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it is necessary that the continuous order of the whole universe also be thrown into confusion. But the providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives their food to beasts, [conjectured: opens his hand] and fills every animal with blessing,^8 and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful grace, could not be forgetful of the human being, whom he created from the beginning in his own image.^9 He who governs all things cares for all things; and he bears providence not only for the human being, but also for all beasts, in whose dominion all things have been placed, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Now, therefore, let us consider how this vast structure of the whole universe somehow persists always in its original disposition and in a most ordered motion. Unless we disgracefully depart from reason, we understand by the plainest reasoning that the immutable divine providence preserves, directs, and governs it. Next, let us contemplate all earthly things: how each and every one is born and proceeds in its natural disposition with the highest order. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created.

Accordingly, the earth has been placed in the middle of the world, like a point or center of its own, which unfolds the circle, and equally distant from the whole universe; nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing, finally, more delightful to the sense could offer itself to be beheld.^10 In this point, enclosed by the immense mass itself, we discern all things wonderfully ordered, and we see that nothing can be left unordered. Thus all things that sometimes seem to us in some way to be drifting, we may know with certainty, in relation to the order of the universe, not to lack their own order. For by the simple and utterly immutable nod of God, the whole mechanism of the entire universe, gathered from so many diverse movable things, harmonizes and is governed in the most ordered fashion. We certainly see, in those matters that fall within our understanding, that the greater intelligence and power arise over time in any governor, the less can anything disorderly happen there by fortuitous chance. Therefore, since that supreme intellect, the creator of all things, the preserver and ruler, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his immutable providence, containing all things under his command, surely no place is ever left for rash chance, which might impede the will of such majesty.

Therefore everything that exists anywhere, or could exist, is comprehended under the command of the one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. Yet unexpected accidents befall us because we are changeable and are changed almost daily [the passage breaks off].^11

^1. “Divine providence” is the controlling theological term of the passage: Trithemius argues that God’s creative will is not merely initial causation but continuing governance, preservation, and ordering of all creatures. ^2. The cited wording corresponds to Judith’s prayer in the Vulgate tradition, especially Judith 9:5-6, where God’s foreknowledge and ordering of events are invoked in a providential frame. ^3. “Ecclesiastes” refers to the Vulgate book associated with Solomon. The citation is Ecclesiastes 5:5 in the Vulgate tradition: the warning not to say “there is no providence” before the angel is especially useful for Trithemius’s anti-fortuna argument. ^4. “Gospel” here introduces a chain of dominical sayings from Matthew, used to move from biblical proof-text to a broader doctrine of providential care. ^5. Matthew 10:29. The “as” is the Roman small copper coin used in the Gospel’s Latin monetary idiom; the argument is that even creatures of negligible market value fall under divine knowledge. ^6. Matthew 6:26. Trithemius uses the Sermon on the Mount’s birds-of-heaven passage to show that providence extends beyond rational creatures. ^7. Matthew 6:30. The “grass of the field” thrown into the oven is a standard Gospel image for transient created things nevertheless adorned by God. ^8. This sentence combines Psalmic language: God gives food to beasts in Psalm 146:9 Vulgate numbering (147:9 in many modern English Bibles), and “opens his hand” and fills every living thing with blessing in Psalm 144:16 Vulgate numbering (145:16 modern). ^9. Genesis 1:26-27. The “image” language is the theological hinge for Trithemius’s a fortiori claim: if God provides for birds, beasts, and flowers, he cannot neglect humanity. ^10. The description assumes a traditional geocentric cosmology: the earth stands at the center-point of the cosmic sphere. Trithemius’s argument here is natural-philosophical rather than observational in the modern scientific sense. ^11. The final sentence is interrupted by the page boundary/OCR excerpt; “unexpected accidents” translates the providential distinction between events unforeseen by mutable human beings and events ordered within the divine mind.

Divine Providence and the Ordering of All Things

Trithemius argues to Emperor Maximilian that God’s immutable intelligence and action extend providentially to every created thing, from the greatest to the smallest, and that the visible order of the world depends on this universal governance.

…having no determinate knowledge of future things. But that best maker of all things, God,^1 since he is wholly immutable, knows all things, beholds all things, and understands all things together and at once.^2 His providence is not deceived; his will is never changed; his power is not broken; his ordinance is not violated; his [unclear] is never interrupted, even if his judgment sometimes seems to be altered.

Therefore, if we attend carefully, we plainly understand that the ends of things and of motion declare that all these lower realities come to be, are preserved, are disposed, and are moved by divine providence.^3 Nothing whatever is alien to his command. For he, God the ruler of all things, understands both all things and each individual thing, not dispersed after our manner among many objects, but abiding in himself as one indivisible being. By contemplating him as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes,^4 [conjectured: he governs the causes of all dangers] and, by knowing all things, cares for them all, directing each by providence toward a good end in an everlasting order.

Come now, most wise Caesar,^5 since we understand divine providence to govern all things, let us join ourselves as briefly as we can to a more focused argument. Thus, if God’s action is his own intelligence, as no wise person will deny, since it is at once most eminent and most inward, then to the extent that he acts he also understands, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in the great, but also in the smallest. Therefore he understands individual things. The influx of the first being^6 is most ample through individual things, whatever their mode of being, as they follow in fixed orders; and the things that act after him are everywhere moved and act by his power.

Either, then, God understands or acts upon nothing outside himself, which is false, or, by acting, he also understands all things and each thing, which is true. For nothing would come to be unless first, to speak in our manner, it were understood by God himself, who makes it; just as those things do not come to be from him which are not brought forth by him.

But because the omnipotent one understands all and each of the things that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, governs, and orders all the things he has made. From him things possess not only the fact that they exist, but also the fact that they are, in a certain way, causes of other things. And so, if things receive from God the capacity to become causes, then from what they have received they also receive the proper office of a cause: that is, to preserve, as far as they can, and to care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes receive this property from the first cause,^7 insofar as they are causes in some sense, then the first cause itself rightly possesses this goodness and providence by nature: namely, that it cares for all things and each thing that it has made, since it is in the highest degree the cause of all and each of them.

Indeed, unless individual things are guarded one by one by him who makes them, the common things that are preserved in individuals will never be guarded. Nor will the whole, which consists of parts, be preserved if those parts themselves are neglected. From the intention of the first, greatest, and common intelligence, therefore, proceeds the universal distinction of things.^8 That intelligence is distinguished by itself from others; the rest are distinguished among themselves by the rule of its own knowledge. Hence, just as God knows all things and each thing most distinctly, so also he most distinctly governs, moderates, and cares for them.

I therefore think, most clement Emperor Maximilian,^9 that it is manifest and sufficiently demonstrated that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, governs, and moderates all lower things both collectively and individually. Otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who observes them, the most beautiful order that we perceive would in no way continue. Nor does it escape me how variously the wise men of this world once [unclear].

^1. “God” here is not merely a devotional designation but the metaphysical subject of the argument: the immutable maker whose knowing, acting, and ordering are treated as inseparable. ^2. “Together and at once” renders the scholastic commonplace that divine cognition is not sequential or discursive but simultaneous; Trithemius contrasts it explicitly with “our manner” of divided attention below. ^3. Divine providence is the central technical term of the passage: not bare foreknowledge, but God’s active governance, conservation, and ordering of created realities toward their ends. ^4. “Cause of causes” is a standard scholastic and Neoplatonic formulation for the first principle from which subordinate causes receive their causal power; the OCR is damaged in the following clause. ^5. “Caesar” addresses Maximilian in imperial style. The dedicatory context is Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, to whom Trithemius directs the argument. ^6. “First being” translates Ens primum, a metaphysical term for God as the primary existent from whom all other beings derive their being and ordered activity. ^7. “First cause” names God as the source not only of created existence but also of secondary causality: creatures can act as causes because causal power is conferred by the primary cause. ^8. “Universal distinction of things” refers to the ordered differentiation of created realities into kinds and individuals, grounded here in the intention and knowledge of the first intelligence. ^9. “Emperor Maximilian” is Maximilian I (1459-1519), Holy Roman Emperor; Trithemius frames the theological proof as an address to a ruler whose office makes providential order politically resonant.

Providence Against Chance and Neglect

Trithemius rejects several opinions that limit or deny divine providence, arguing from Boethius, Scripture, Lactantius, Anselm, and Aristotelian philosophy that God governs all things, including corruptible particulars.

Wise men have held differing opinions about providence.^1 Some of them thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance. If their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence; rather, everything would necessarily drift without order, since the world, just as it had been made by chance, could also perish by chance.

Against their false opinion others have taught that the world could neither have been made without reason nor continue in existence with any certainty unless it were governed by the providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, sower of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity and, remaining stable, give all things motion.”^2 And again he said that the generation of all things, all the processes of mutable nature, and whatever is moved, draw their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly bodies, separate substances, and also the species of things, while he knew nothing at all of everything else and wholly neglected it.^3 But they erred shamefully, because the almighty has providence and care not only for universals and incorruptibles, but also for particulars and corruptibles. Hence holy Boethius again says that the exalted creator sits upon the earth, rules things and bends the reins, king and lord, source and origin, law and wise judge of equity. He is the continuous love for all things, and they seek to be held by the end of the good, because they cannot endure otherwise unless, by love turned back again, the causes which he himself gave flow back to him.^4

Others, unable to bear the thought that they themselves were neglected, exempted the human being from the number of corruptible things because of the preeminence of the intellect, saying that God has care and providence for human beings but despises all other earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has already been said, and to bring forward many further arguments would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord” [conjectured: save].^5 And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has equal care for all.”^6 Therefore divine majesty, by its providence, orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all lower things, both collectively and individually: great and small, corruptible and incorruptible. Its most powerful will brought all things forth from nothing, as sacred Scripture again testifies: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.”^7

Let men of corrupted mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, be ashamed: swollen with empty talk, they take away the providence of the one who knows all things, and they do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For, to use the judgment of Firmianus, what is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence?^8 But if he provides for nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has now lost all his dignity. Yet it is impossible, as Saint Anselm attests, for God to lose his honor,^9 because, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, no corruption, and no sin.^10 Therefore whoever removes providence removes the whole substance of God, and this is as if he said that God does not exist.

But let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things now tell me this. If God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is henceforth no reason for us to pursue him with worship or venerate him with religion on account of any benefit; rather, being neglected and despised, we should neglect him in return. But if, not knowing us, he despises us, [unclear].

^1. “Providence” translates providentia, here the theological doctrine that divine intellect and will order creation; the passage opposes both Epicurean-style chance and restricted models of divine governance. ^2. Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy III, metrum 9, where divine governance is described through God’s stable eternity and the ordered motion of time and the cosmos. Trithemius cites Boethius as “most Christian,” reflecting medieval reception of Boethius as a Christian philosophical authority. ^3. “Separate substances” (substantiae separatae) are immaterial intelligences in Aristotelian and scholastic metaphysics; in Christian usage they are often identified or correlated with angels. The view rejected here limits providence to celestial and universal realities. ^4. The second Boethian citation evokes the Consolation’s cosmological account of love and order: created causes endure by returning toward the good that is their source. The OCR is damaged, but the philosophical sense is recoverable from Boethian diction. ^5. Psalm 35:7 in the Vulgate numbering, corresponding to Psalm 36:6 in many English Bibles: “humans and beasts you save, Lord.” Trithemius uses the verse to deny that providence is restricted to rational creatures. ^6. Wisdom of Solomon 6:7: “the small and the great he made, and he has equal care for all.” This is one of Trithemius’s central proof-texts for providence over particulars. ^7. Wisdom of Solomon 14:3, “your providence, Father, governs,” here expanded in Trithemius’s wording to cover all things “from the beginning.” ^8. “Firmianus” is Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius, whose Divine Institutes repeatedly argues against denial of providence and presents providential rule as proper to the one God. ^9. Anselm’s claim that God cannot lose his honor recalls the logic of Cur Deus Homo, where divine honor and justice cannot be diminished in reality, even when creatures fail to render what they owe. ^10. “The Peripatetic” is Aristotle, so called from the Peripatetic school. The maxim that eternal things admit neither evil nor corruption is used here to support divine immutability and incorruptibility.

Divine Providence and the Collapse of Piety

Trithemius argues that denial of divine providence destroys the grounds of worship, Christian faith, civic order, and hope, and he reasserts that all creation is governed by God’s care.

[unclear] despises and neglects [unclear], there is now no cause at all for us to worship, or to invoke with prayers, one who does not know us and who for that reason can confer no good upon us. For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause of piety ceases, since he would himself be no source of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence^1 is removed, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, then surely he neither bestows benefits upon human beings nor imposes punishments upon deserters; he neither can nor wishes to aid mortals; he does not care at all, does not notice what we do, and hears neither the prayers nor the petitions of anyone. Why, then, do we offer him any worship? Why honor? Why prayers? Or why do we so greatly revere or fear a God who does not know us? Since he neglects and despises us, he can do us neither good nor harm. For once providence is removed, neither holiness nor religion remains; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and a dreadful confusion will follow. Once piety toward God has been removed, what will the commonwealth^2 be except everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings will necessarily perish, and with it the fellowship of the human race; all justice likewise will vanish and perish at the same time. What is to be thought of the Christian faith^3 if God does not care for human affairs? Finally, what is to be thought of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of all,^4 except that the whole matter will be considered an empty fable and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? For whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and of no worth to us, if he has no care at all for us.

Those who deny the providence of God now see and shudder, when they look upon the end of their opinion: the worst despair of all. Let no one, therefore, led on by the empty talk of secular philosophers,^5 train himself to contempt for God. Let no one take away the providence of the highest and unchangeable Good.^6 Let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of and ungrateful for the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole world,^7 visible as well as invisible, and all things individually, whether they are in heaven, on earth, or in the sea,^8 are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is alien to his care. For crops and all the other things that the earth brings forth, storms too, the varieties of the seasons, and changes of the heavens by which all things that the earth naturally produces come to maturity, are provided by divine providence for the human race: all things collectively and individually, not only the great but also the smallest, to such a degree that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father,^9 who created it, rules it, and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this vast magnitude of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by the one God, who alone exists [as God], he is greatly mistaken, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. Indeed, the one who could bring the whole world into being from nothing^10 can also govern forever, by his own providence, what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, and can do all things: he alone, omnipotent, created all things.

Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel,^11 should above all venerate divine providence, and with whatever strength we can, lift our minds upward [unclear].

^1. “Providence” here is not Trithemius’s angelic-period theory of the secundei, but the broader theological claim that God actively governs and cares for created things. ^2. Respublica denotes the ordered civic community or commonwealth; Trithemius presents providence as the foundation not only of private devotion but of public trust, social bonds, and justice. ^3. The argument is apologetic: if providence is denied, Christian doctrine loses its basis because salvation, punishment, prayer, and divine beneficence all presuppose God’s active care. ^4. Jesus Christ is invoked as salvator omnium, “Savior of all,” in a providential frame: Christ’s saving work would be reduced to fiction if God did not care for mortal affairs. ^5. “Secular philosophers” translates Philosophi saeculares, a polemical label for non-Christian or insufficiently Christian philosophical arguments when they are taken to undermine providence. ^6. “The highest and unchangeable Good” is a Christian-Platonic formulation for God, emphasizing both supreme goodness and immutability. ^7. “This whole world” translates hunc mundum universum as apparently intended by the OCR’s modum vniuersum; the visible/invisible pairing echoes standard creedal and Pauline language. ^8. “In heaven, on earth, or in the sea” recalls biblical merisms for the totality of creation, especially the commandment formula in Exodus 20:11 and the doxological language of Revelation 5:13. ^9. The falling leaf is not a direct Gospel quotation but functions like Matthew 10:29, where not even a sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father; Trithemius intensifies the point by applying it to a leaf. ^10. Creation “from nothing” translates the scholastic theological doctrine creatio ex nihilo, grounding God’s continuing governance in his original creative power. ^11. “The holy Gospel” marks the explicitly Christian authority for the preceding providential claims, especially prayer, salvation, and the Father’s care for even the smallest created things.

Providence and Trithemius’s Protestation to Maximilian

Trithemius concludes his proof that the world is governed by divine providence and appends a formal declaration of Catholic orthodoxy and submission to Roman ecclesiastical judgment.

[unclear] from those things that are perishable, and, having been brought back to ourselves, let us be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God^1 as present everywhere. Since that majesty is altogether uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. It does not sustain from one side and surpass from another; nor does it fill from one side and encompass from another. Rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. God is nowhere present by the mass of a body, and by his uncircumscribable substance is nowhere absent. He is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in the purity of the heart.^2

O inexplicable power, O incomprehensible mercy, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity: you are not composed of parts, as a body is; you are not distinguished by affections, as a soul is; you are not subject to forms, as are all other things that have been made through you. You are in all things and above all things, most wisely ruling and governing the universe.

By these testimonies, most sacred Caesar Maximilian,^3 it has, I think, been sufficiently proved that this whole world is governed by the providence of God.^4 Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and everlasting, he knows all things, understands all things, and foreknows all things. Since he is omnipotent by nature, he can do all things that are possible; for him nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. He who created such wondrous things by his power establishes them in truth, perfects them by reason, sustains them by virtue, and illumines them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory: he who lives and reigns as glorious and exalted God forever and ever. Amen.

The Author’s Protestation to Caesar

These, most unconquered Caesar Maximilian, are the things that seemed to me necessary to say in response to the eight questions proposed by your majesty.^5 For you wished to have my judgment on those same questions in writing, making an assessment of me above the truth: I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before mine. Let your pardon make me worthy, if I have said anything less than proper, since, at the command of your highness, I dictated what occurred to me by way of reply as best I could, at intervals, while set as a traveler upon a journey.

I state, moreover, from my mind and openly protest that I am a sincere confessor of the Christian faith^6 and that I wish to remain, even to death, in union with the sacrosanct Roman Church.^7 Therefore, if anything either in this lucubration or in any other work has been said or written by me otherwise than she holds, judges, believes, and teaches, I, as a true son of obedience, denounce it by this present attestation and wish it simply to be, and perpetually to be held as, revoked.^8

For this reason, most wise Caesar, I both humbly ask and urgently admonish your majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are said to be destined, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For the greatest care must be taken that nothing be proposed to those whose salvation your Serenity watches over unless it is solid, tested, manifest, and legitimately confirmed in the Catholic faith by the opinion of many wise men.

May almighty God by his providence direct and always preserve you, Maximilian, greatest of emperors, to the praise of his name. From the city of Neumarkt,^9 on the tenth day of the month of July, in the Christian year 1508.^10

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.^11

^1. The passage closes the theological argument of the Liber Octo Quaestionum by grounding universal governance in God’s omnipresence and uncircumscribable being, a standard scholastic idiom for divine immensity. ^2. “Seen through faith in purity of heart” evokes Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” while distinguishing spiritual perception from bodily sight. ^3. Maximilian I, king of the Romans from 1486 and Holy Roman Emperor-elect from 1508; Trithemius addresses him as the patron who posed the eight questions. ^4. “Providence” here is theological rather than astrological determinism: God’s foreknowledge and governance remain the final cause and regulator of the whole created order. ^5. The “eight questions” are the organizing frame of the Liber Octo Quaestionum, a set of replies written for Maximilian on theological and providential matters. ^6. Trithemius’s explicit confession of Christian faith functions as an orthodoxy clause, especially important given his interests in angelology, occult philosophy, and hidden writing. ^7. The Roman Church is invoked as the binding doctrinal authority against which the work is to be judged. ^8. “Lucubration” means a work composed by night or in spare hours; the revocation formula is a conventional early-modern safeguard submitting all statements to ecclesiastical correction. ^9. “Neometana” is Neumarkt, here most likely Neumarkt in der Oberpfalz, where Trithemius stayed during periods of travel after leaving Sponheim. ^10. The date is 10 July 1508, given in the “year of the Christians” rather than by a regnal or indictional system. ^11. Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Benedictine abbot and humanist scholar, was formerly abbot of Sponheim and later abbot of St James at Würzburg; the signature preserves his abbatial identity.
